name: Twitch Plays Pokémon
title: A Million People Played One Game of Pokémon
claims: Twitch Plays Pokémon is a social experiment and channel on Twitch where crowdsourced users play Nintendo Pokémon games by sending chat commands | 1
It holds the Guinness World Record for having the most users to input a command to play a live streamed videogame with 1,165,140 participants | 1
The concept was developed by an anonymous Australian programmer and launched on 12 February 2014 with Pokémon Red | 1
The stream reached an average concurrent viewership of over 80,000 viewers with at least 10% participating | 1
The game was completed on 1 March 2014 after more than 16 continuous days of gameplay | 1
Twitch estimated over 1.16 million people participated with peak simultaneous participation at 121,000 and 55 million total views | 1
On 5 December 2014, Twitch Plays Pokémon received a Game Award in the Best Fan Creation category | 1
The experiment gained attention for its interactivity, erratic nature, unique challenges, and community-developed memes | 1
Twitch used the experiment to explore making streaming more interactive | 1
The broadcaster continued the channel with other Pokémon games and unofficial ROM hacks as long as interest remained | 1
The success led to similar Twitch-based streams for other games | 1
The system was inspired by Salty Bet and coded by an anonymous Australian programmer known as the Streamer | 1
The system used an IRC bot written in Python and the Game Boy emulator VisualBoyAdvance | 1
The script captures case-insensitive messages (directional commands, B, A, select, start) and sends them to the emulator as button input | 1
A JavaScript web app displays a live tally of moves shown within the stream | 1
The Streamer chose Pokémon Red and Blue due to nostalgia, the belief that progress is easy even when played poorly, and its forgiving turn-based structure | 1
An edited version of the game claiming to make all 151 Pokémon accessible was used, though it was unfinished and had no gameplay differences | 1
The control scheme made the game longer and harder, causing Red to get stuck in corners, walk in circles, and compulsively check the Pokédex and save | 1
Areas involving mazes and ledges caused recurring difficulties, with ledges taking several hours due to users intentionally spamming "down" | 1
An incident called "Bloody Sunday" involved the accidental release of twelve Pokémon while trying to obtain a Zapdos from the PC | 1
Users repeatedly sent "start" commands to open the pause menu and inventory, leading to a system to throttle Start button inputs | 1
Players attempted to collaborate through infographics and a user script that hid command messages to allow conversation | 1
A computer program was created to automatically identify trolls | 1
The Streamer collaborated with others to continue preparing tools and live commentary | 1
The Streamer stepped down from his role on 22 November 2017 due to intra-group hostility and gave control to another collaborator | 1
On 18 February 2014, Democracy mode was introduced for the Team Rocket hideout puzzle | 1
Democracy mode tallied all inputs over a period (usually 30 seconds) and executed the winning command; users could append numbers like "right3" | 1
Outrage and protest broke out in chat using the "start9" command to fight the system, known as "The start9 protests" | 1
The broadcaster reworked Democracy mode so users could vote between Anarchy and Democracy modes via an on-screen meter | 1
Democracy mode required a supermajority vote, while Anarchy mode required a majority vote | 1
Democracy mode was considered divisive by players who felt it conflicted with the original concept and eliminated randomness | 1
On 2 March 2014, Pokémon Crystal began with a developer-set deadline and Democracy mode automatically activated at the top of each hour | 1
Players reached Mt. Silver to battle Red on 14 March 2014, with Red's team modified to match the party used to beat the Elite Four in the Red playthrough | 1
Crystal was beaten on 15 March after more than 13 days of playtime | 1
Pokémon Emerald started on 21 March 2014 with Democracy mode initially disabled entirely, and was repeatedly restarted due to soft resets before being fixed | 1
Pokémon X was played using actual hardware via a hard-mod known as 3xtDS (3DS Streaming Console with External Control Interface), developed by Reddit user dekuNukem | 1
The 3xtDS mod allowed direct USB-based inputs, video output capture, and internet-enabled features like online battles, trades, and O-Powers | 1
Pokémon Omega Ruby was also played on the stream | 1
In February 2015, a new run of Red began to complete the main storyline and catch all 151 Pokémon, which took around 39 days | 1
For the fourth anniversary, the channel started simultaneous playthroughs of Red and Blue with alternating commands and shared Democracy mode inputs | 1
As the experiment moved into its fifth and sixth years, the channel used fan-created mods and ran a gauntlet of six games in a row | 1
The stream launched on 12 February 2014 and was relatively inactive for the first day and a half before going viral | 1
By 14 February, total viewership reached around 175,000 as players beat the first of eight Gym leaders | 1
By 17 February, the channel reached over 6.5 million total views | 1
By 20 February, total views exceeded 17 million, with concurrent viewership between 60 and 70 thousand and at least 10% participating | 1
By 20 February, players had caught 12 species of Pokémon and passed the fourth gym | 1
Upon completing Red, total views reached 36 million, peak concurrent viewership hit 120,000, and an estimated 658,000 had participated | 1
The high activity caused enormous stress on Twitch's chat system, requiring engineers to move chat to a higher-capacity e-sports server | 1
The developer noted he did not expect the stream to become so overwhelmingly popular | 1
An active community emerged on Reddit liveblogging proceedings and developing memes | 1
The Helix Fossil was an inventory item selected so frequently it became an inside joke and was treated as a player "religion" or deity representing Anarchy mode | 1
The Dome Fossil was treated as a deity for those supporting Democracy mode, and fans published "bibles" for the Helix religion | 1
Captured Pokémon gained fan followings: ABBBBBBK( (Charmeleon) and JLVWNNOOOO (Rattata) were nicknamed Abby and Jay Leno | 1
The team's Pidgeot was named "Bird Jesus", and the Zapdos was nicknamed "AA-j", "Archangel of Justice", or "Anarchy Bird" | 1
The team's Flareon was dubbed the "False Prophet" because it was accidentally obtained instead of Vaporeon for "Surf" and caused the release of Abby and Jay Leno | 1
On Sunday, 23 February (eleventh day), players inadvertently released a dozen Pokémon | 1
The creator described the stream as a "social experiment" streaming an emulated version of Pokémon Red to Twitch.tv | 2
Commands like "up", "down", "left", "right", "a", "b", or "start" led to onscreen actions after 20 to 40 seconds depending on video lag | 2
Progress was possible early on, with the internet hivemind catching a team and clearing four of eight gyms in the first four days | 2
The game got stuck in Team Rocket's lair with over 50,000 players issuing delayed commands | 2
Salty Bet is another Twitch game where spectators bet fake money on randomized M.U.G.E.N. matches | 2
Much of the appeal of Twitch Plays Pokémon is the fan community, memes, and imitators | 2
The author noted the bone-deep sadness felt when Charmeleon was released four days and nine hours in | 2
The author suggested the stream is a summary of the human condition where people struggle and fail to accomplish basic tasks | 2
Democracy mode was added to curb trolls and get past the Team Rocket hideout | 2

sources.title: The bizarre, mind-numbing, mesmerizing beauty of “Twitch Plays Pokémon” - Ars Technica
